notes.meaning: The Lord tells Samuel to stop grieving over Saul, because God has firmly rejected him from being king over Israel. Samuel is told to fill an animal horn with oil and travel to Bethlehem, where God has chosen one of Jesse's sons to be the next ruler. God's good purposes do not end when human leaders fail.

Samuel worries that Saul will hear about his mission and execute him for treason. God tells him to take a heifer along and announce that he is coming to offer a sacrifice to the Lord. Offering this sacrifice was completely true, and concealing the secret anointing kept Samuel safe without telling a lie.

God directs Samuel to invite Jesse and his family to the sacrificial feast. Once there, God promises to show Samuel exactly which son to anoint. God guides His servants step by step as they walk in obedience.

Samuel obeys the Lord and arrives in the small town of Bethlehem. The city leaders tremble when they meet him, fearing that the great prophet has come to judge some secret crime or that his visit will anger King Saul.

Samuel calms their fears by explaining that he comes in peace to offer a sacrifice. He tells the leaders to consecrate themselves, which meant washing their clothes and bodies and preparing their hearts to meet God in worship. Samuel also gives special care to preparing Jesse and his sons for the holy feast.
When the sons arrive, Samuel looks at Jesse's oldest son, Eliab. Seeing his tall build and impressive looks, Samuel immediately assumes this must be the man God has chosen to be king.

The Lord corrects Samuel and tells him not to judge by Eliab's height or good looks, because God has not chosen him. Human beings can only see the outside, but God looks straight into the heart. God values inner faith, love, and obedience far more than outward charm.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest the Hebrew text suffered a minor copying omission here, and they follow ancient Greek translations that supply the missing words to read, 'for God does not see as man sees.'

notes.meaning: Jesse brings his second son, Abinadab, and has him walk past Samuel. Samuel listens for God's guidance and announces that the Lord has not chosen him either.
Jesse next presents his third son, Shammah. Once again, Samuel confirms that the Lord has not chosen this son.

Jesse presents seven of his sons before the prophet, but God passes over all of them. Samuel tells Jesse that the Lord has chosen none of these young men. God does not hand out His callings based on birth order or human expectations.

Samuel asks Jesse if he has any other sons. Jesse admits that the youngest is still outside looking after the sheep, as his family had not even thought to invite him. Samuel insists that no one will sit down to eat the feast until the boy arrives.

Jesse sends for his youngest son, who comes in from the pastures. He has a healthy, reddish complexion, bright eyes, and a pleasing appearance. The Lord whispers to Samuel to stand up and anoint him, because this young shepherd is God's chosen king.

Samuel takes the horn of oil and pours it on David in the presence of his family, marking him out for future royal service. Right away, the Holy Spirit rushes upon David with power to give him wisdom and courage from that day forward, after which Samuel returns home to Ramah.

The special enabling presence of the Lord's Spirit leaves Saul, and God allows a troubling spirit to torment him with deep gloom, fear, and bursts of rage. When a person turns away from God, they lose His peaceful guidance and become open to misery.

differ.view: Saul was never truly born again, so the Spirit's departure was not a loss of salvation, but the removal of God's temporary gifts and power for ruling.
In the Old Testament the Holy Spirit came upon leaders for specific tasks and could depart, unlike the permanent indwelling that believers receive today.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The phrase translated 'evil spirit' can simply mean a harmful, injurious spirit of depression or emotional breakdown that God sent as a punishment, rather than a demon.

notes.meaning: Saul's royal servants notice the sudden change in his behavior and speak honestly to him. They tell him plainly that his deep torment is coming from a troubling spirit permitted by God.

The servants suggest that Saul order them to find a skilled harp player. They explain that playing peaceful music will calm the king's troubled emotions and restore his peace of mind when the distress comes over him.
Saul accepts their advice and commands his staff to look for a gifted musician. He tells them to bring the player to court without delay.

One of the servants speaks up and recommends David, the son of Jesse from Bethlehem. He describes David not only as a talented harpist, but also as a brave and sensible man, handsome, and clearly blessed with the Lord's presence.

Saul sends royal messengers to Jesse with a direct command to send his son David, who is out watching the flock. Even after being anointed, David had humbly returned to his ordinary chores in the fields.
Jesse prepares a respectful gift for the king according to the customs of the time. He loads a donkey with bread, a skin of wine, and a young goat, and sends them to Saul with David.
David arrives at court and enters the king's presence to serve him. Saul likes the young man very much and gives him the trusted post of armor-bearer, placing him close to the throne.
Saul sends another message to Jesse, asking permission for David to remain permanently in the royal court. Saul explains that he is deeply pleased with David and wants him nearby.
Whenever the troubling spirit comes upon Saul, David takes his harp and plays songs of praise. The sweet music calms Saul's mind, bringing him great relief, and the dark spirit leaves him for a time.
